## What you'll be able to do

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Apply the *grammar of graphics* framework to construct statistical plots
- Build the **5 named graphs** (scatterplots, linegraphs, histograms, boxplots, barplots) using `ggplot2`
- Modify aesthetic properties of a plot (color, size, transparency, position)
- Use *facets* to split a plot into panels by a categorical variable

::: {.predict}
Before we begin: which of these objectives feels least familiar to you right now? Hold that in mind — we'll check back at the end.
:::

Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.

::: {.mcq data-correct="c"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q1. Which component of the grammar of graphics is responsible for telling `ggplot2` *what kind* of mark to draw (points, bars, lines)?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>data</li>
  <li>aesthetic mapping (`aes`)</li>
  <li>geometric object (`geom`)</li>
  <li>facet</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(c)</strong> `geom_*()` functions specify the visual mark; `aes()` is the mapping between data and visual properties; `data` is the data frame.</div>
:::

## Check-in: 5NG#2: Linegraphs

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q4. A student writes `geom_point(aes(alpha = 0.2))` expecting all points to be 20% opaque. Instead, they get an unexpected legend showing alpha values. Why?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>`aes()` always creates a legend</li>
  <li>Inside `aes()`, the value `0.2` is interpreted as a *variable name* — ggplot tries to map a fictional column named `0.2` to alpha</li>
  <li>Alpha must be between 0 and 1</li>
  <li>`geom_point()` doesn't support alpha</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> **Constants belong OUTSIDE `aes()`.** `aes(alpha = 0.2)` says &quot;map the (nonexistent) variable `0.2` to alpha&quot;. The fix: `geom_point(alpha = 0.2)` *sets* alpha as a constant. Same logic for `color`, `size`, `shape`, etc.</div>
:::

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q5. What is the difference between `geom_bar()` and `geom_col()`?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>They're identical</li>
  <li>`geom_bar()` counts rows for you (no `y` needed); `geom_col()` expects pre-computed bar heights mapped to `y`</li>
  <li>`geom_col()` makes a column chart only; `geom_bar()` makes a row chart</li>
  <li>`geom_col()` is deprecated</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Use `geom_bar()` when each row in your data is one observation to be tallied (e.g., one row per flight). Use `geom_col()` when the data is already summarized (you have explicit `y` values).</div>
:::

## Check-in: 5NG#4: Boxplots

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q7. In `ggplot()`, why must the `+` come at the **end** of a line, not the beginning of the next?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Convention only</li>
  <li>R's parser treats `+` at start-of-line as continuing an arithmetic expression that may not be in scope; ending lines with `+` signals &quot;I'm not done yet&quot;</li>
  <li>RStudio adds it automatically</li>
  <li>Both placements are valid</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> R reads code line by line. Ending a line with `+` tells the parser the statement isn't complete. Starting a line with `+` would make R think the previous line was complete and now you're starting a fresh expression that begins with `+` (an error).</div>
:::

Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.

::: {.mcq data-correct="d"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q8. A scatterplot of `dep_delay` vs `arr_delay` shows a dense black blob near (0, 0). Which technique does **NOT** address overplotting?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Setting `alpha = 0.1` for transparency</li>
  <li>Using `geom_jitter()` to perturb each point slightly</li>
  <li>Subsetting the data to fewer observations</li>
  <li>Adding more bins to the plot</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(d)</strong> Bins are a histogram concept; scatterplots don't have bins. The other three are real overplotting remedies — alpha makes density visible, jitter spreads coincident points, subsetting reduces overlap.</div>
:::
